newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire rebel meets U.N. envoy, rejects ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel meets U.N. envoy, rejects ceasefire.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila met U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun on Thursday in the northern Ugandan town of Gulu but rejected pleas for a ceasefire, diplomats said on Friday.

The diplomats, told Reuters by telephone from the Ugandan capital that the meeting in the war-torn outpost was hosted by Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, who is in Gulu supervising a government offensive against Sudan-backed Ugandan rebels.

A regional military source told Reuters the meeting came as Kabila's rebels advanced on the lakeside town of Pweto in the mineral-rich Shaba province and consolidated their positions on several fronts around Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city.

The diplomats said Museveni, a regional power broker accused by Zaire of backing Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, facilitated the face-to-face meeting but did not take sides.
"They (Kabila and Sahnoun) met in Gulu in talks chaired by Museveni but Kabila bluntly refused to commit himself to a ceasefire of any kind," a diplomat said.

Another diplomat who closely monitored the secret meeting added: "Kabila said he did not see any logic in a ceasefire while (Zairean President) Mobutu Sese Seko refused to deal with the rebel group or at least issue guarantees for talks."

Sahnoun is mandated by the U.N. Security Council and the Organisation of African Unity to lead efforts to end the fighting in Zaire and find a political settlement there and in the surrounding "Great Lakes" region of Central Africa.
Kabila, advancing on Kisangani in a challenge to Mobutu who is ailing in France, has accepted a U.N. peace plan as a basis for talks but rejected its call for a ceasefire.
"He (Kabila) says he sees no point in committing his group to a ceasefire while Kinshasa gives mixed signals and vows to settle the matter militarily," another diplomat said.
On Thursday, France called on the international community to consider setting up a "security framework" for Zaire -- code words for a multinational intervention force.

"If there is no ceasefire, the international community must consider setting up a security framework (to help delivery of) humanitarian aid," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a news briefing.
But at a Brussels meeting of high-level officials from the 15-nation European Union, the French call got a cool reception.

Kabila's rebels have made significant gains and a regional military source said on Friday they were advancing on the town of Pweto on Lake Tanganyika in the mineral-rich Shaba province. He said rebels had also consolidated positions around Kisangani.
Kisangani -- a diamond and gold centre on River Zaire -- is the biggest prize in Africa's latest war while Shaba is highly strategic because of rich copper and cobalt deposits.
"We have detected major movements towards Pweto and the rebels are being aided by Kabila's popular support in that area," the source said.
"Around Kisangani, we have detected massive consolidation by the rebels but no major action yet. Movement towards Kisangani appears to have been slowed down by heavy mining of the area," he added.
Zaire accuses Rwanda and Uganda of sponsoring Kabila's rebels and deploying troops in the eastern war zone. They deny the charge.
